title: First Year Wrap & Major Wins
subtext: Wrapped up year one with wins at Techtrix and Hackforge.

blocks.text: The title says it all—this is the first-year wrap. But here’s the thing: the story isn’t finished yet.
So far, I’ve shared a bit of the madness in this LinkedIn post:
Here’s a quick TL;DR

Two major hackathon wins, a flurry of events, and a whole lot of chaos in between. From coding on zero sleep to surviving on caffeine, it's been non-stop action. I’ve pulled off some cool stuff, taken part in everything from cryptography challenges to pitching competitions, and somehow managed to keep learning through it all.
But this is still in progress. The full story is unfolding in real time—as you're reading this, I’m probably out there, doing another random event or cooking up something new.
So yeah, stay tuned.

title: Hackathon Era Begins
subtext: Built AcadZ at HackSynthesis and kept grinding at Hack<N>Pitch and Diversion2k25.

blocks.text: This was the comeback arc. Time to step back up and be the 100x dev I was always meant to be.

It all kicked off with Hack Synthesis, where we built AcadZ — a student-focused mobile app. My first real hackathon experience. I remember staying up all night trying to figure out how to call the Gemini API. I was completely fried, running on caffeine and vibes. But the energy? Unreal. The food? Biryani. Actual cinema.
After that, the next few months were all gas, no brakes.

Hackathons. Tech events. Competitions. Free food. Fire merch. At some point, I wasn’t sure if I was going for the code or the coffee mugs. Maybe both. Still, it was one of the most intense, fulfilling, chaotic, and beautiful stretches I’ve had.
You can go deep in these posts if you want the details:
But here’s the TL;DR if you’re lazy:
First Hackathon Season Highlights

items: Built Naval Vanguard with team WhiteSpace at a naval hackathon. Maritime monitoring with LLMs, NLP, maps, threat analysis — the works.
Got introduced to machine learning and participated in a Kaggle challenge, building a URL classifier with XGBoost.
GameDev India Campfire (connected with indie devs + shared my journey)
Blockchain Day (solved the challenge, got my first event T-shirt)
Built Hacktivate, a full-stack hackathon management platform using Next.js, FastAPI & Hugging Face Llama at Hack<N>Pitch.
Went to DevFest 2024 (food, venue, people = peak)
Zero Trust: made an AI fraud detection system using Graph Neural Networks
Cooked up a dumb, genius idea called “The Brainrot Defense Mechanism Against AI” with memes and chaos at Abol Tabol (got Ohio-diffed, no regrets)
At Diversion, my first MLH hackathon, built Cryptonian — a Web3-powered edtech platform (Gemini API + Aptos + MongoDB + Streamlit). Went sleepless for 36 hours with a killer team.

blocks.text: All that wrapped up my first semester of college.

Before this, I was the reserved school kid. Now I’m out here coding at midnight, pitching AI projects, pulling off unhinged builds, vibing with people I didn’t even know a few months ago. It’s been real.

title: Team XCeption & HackHeritage Setback
subtext: Put everything into HackHeritage 2024 but didn’t qualify — still a huge learning curve.

blocks.text: Just joined college. Feeling good. The best part? The JEE grind was finally over.
Met some cool people, and soon enough, we found out about HackHeritage—our college’s internal hackathon to select teams for the Smart India Hackathon (SIH).
This was going to be my first proper hackathon. 6 people. 24 hours. Overnight on campus. Chaos.

Forming the team was a mission in itself. We interviewed people. Literally conducted interviews to find first-year students with solid dev experience because we wanted to build a proper all-first-year lineup. After a ton of back-and-forth, we finally formed Team XCeption.
But we took so long building the team that we barely had any time to prep.
Picking a problem statement from SIH’s massive list was another nightmare—tons of research, zero hackathon experience, and no clue what we were diving into.

HackHeritage had a selection round too. You had to submit a presentation pitching your solution first. Only then would you be allowed to build anything. We rushed to finish the deck just minutes before the deadline. Showed up in formals. Pitched early. Then waited.
And waited.
Finally, they released the list of selected teams.
We scrolled. We searched.
No XCeption.
We didn’t make it.
After everything—the work, the team-building, the pitch prep—we didn’t even get to do the hackathon.
It sucked. Genuinely broke me for a while.
At first, we had no clue what went wrong. But looking back, I realized where we slipped. It was a hard pill to swallow, but it was also the wake-up call I needed.
In school, I used to think I was good at this coding thing. But college made it clear—I had a long way to go.
Still, this was just one setback. And setbacks are what push you forward.

title: JEE Grind to HITK
subtext: Took a step back from building, cracked JEE, and joined HITK for CSBS.

blocks.text: Honestly, talking about this feels like asking a World War II veteran to recount the trenches. It was brutal.
Development pretty much came to a halt during this phase. But deep down, I knew—once I got into college, I was going to go all in on dev. That kept me going.
Two whole years, just gone. Can’t really say they were well spent, but hey—I made it. Cracked the damn thing, got into HITK.
And this? This is where the real journey kicks off.

title: The Game Dev Phase
subtext: Made two games, joined Brackeys Game Jam 2021.2, then built two more with friends.

blocks.text: Unironically one of the biggest phases of my life. Even though I haven’t made a game in over two years, I still proudly call myself a game dev. (Yeah I know, I gotta get back into it. Crying emoji IRL.)

It all started when some of my friends were like, “Let’s learn Unity.” We were already nerds who loved playing games, and now we were nerds who knew how to code. Naturally, the next logical step was to try making our own.
So, I did what every beginner did — binged Brackeys' 3D game tutorial. After following along, I ended up building two small games from scratch. Never published them, but they taught me a lot.
Brackeys Game Jam 2021.2
This was my first real game jam — and holy hell, it was a blast.

I put in hours every single day: learning Unity, trying Blender for the first time (which was a disaster), designing levels, and debugging like a madman. I made everything in the game myself — including the janky-ass 3D models. My PC back then was such a potato that adding a few extra vertices in Blender would cause it to combust. So everything had to stay low-poly as hell.
Still, I managed to finish and submit the game. It was a basic shooter with a little platformer level at the end. Graphics were trash, but I was proud.

Then came the post-jam experience — the community. I’d spend hours rating other people’s games, reading comments, and watching feedback roll in. I even [speedran one of the jam entries](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WW5h6-upy4Y) and posted the run on YouTube just for fun.
The final stats?
Yeah not great, but hey — first game ever. It meant the world to me.
The Games That Followed
After that jam, I worked on two more games with friends:

items: [Project Addax](https://letsbecool.itch.io/project-addax) — my first time working with a team on a Brackeys jam. Absolute chaos trying to coordinate, but I learned a lot about collaboration.
[Boka Robi](https://aliensearth.itch.io/boka-robi) — a brainrotted, cursed game made in one day at a friend’s house. No plan, just vibes.

blocks.text: And just like that, my game dev arc was in full swing. I miss this shit. Definitely need to get back into it.

title: The Origin Story
subtext: Started coding in class 8, found joy in school-level dev and DSA.

blocks.text: Back in class 8, I got into coding the way every legend starts — with a school-assigned Java textbook, BlueJ, and a diary I turned into my own dev journal. Yeah, we literally coded on paper during class. When things got boring, my friends and I would just start scribbling Java code in our copies like absolute nerds — and I fucking loved it.
Later at home, I'd run those scribbles on my PC, see them actually work, and mess around making small changes. That shit felt like magic. I was hooked.
That’s when I realized: this isn’t just homework. This is fun.

I started learning basic DSA stuff from YouTube (no ChatGPT back in the day, mind you). Picked up both Java and Python, trying out different problems and figuring out the logic behind them. It was all self-taught, all curiosity-fueled. No pressure. Just pure love for building things with code.
